question.:question/worked-solution:
We apply the power rule with $n=20$, and we get

$$
\int {x}^{20}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{20+1}}{20+1}+C=\frac{{x}^{21}}{21}+C.
$$

Let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{21}}{21}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{21}}{21})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{1}{21}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{21})+0 & = \\ \frac{1}{21}\cdot 21{x}^{20} & = \\ {x}^{20}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{'}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{'}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{'}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We apply the power rule with $n=17$, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{17}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{17+1}}{17+1}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{18}}{18}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{18}}{18}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{18}}{18})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{1}{18}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{18})+0 & = \\ \frac{1}{18}\cdot 18\,{x}^{17} & = \\ {x}^{17}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

We start by writing the root as a rational power, $\sqrt{x}={x}^{1/2}.$ So, we can apply the power rule with $n=\frac{1}{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{1/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{1/2+1}}{(\frac{1}{2}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3/2}}{(\frac{3}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{2}{3}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3/2})+0 & = \\ \frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{3}{2}{x}^{3/2-1} & = \\ {x}^{1/2}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Antiderivative of a Reciprocal Function

question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can use the power rule with $n=-\frac{1}{7}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{-1/7}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-1/7+1}}{(-\frac{1}{7}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{6/7}}{(\frac{6}{7})}+C \\  & =\frac{7}{6}{x}^{6/7}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Integrating Sums of Power Functions

question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the sum and constant factor rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}& \int\left(x^{2}-\sqrt{x}+2\right)\,\mathrm{d}x\\ &= \int\left(x^{2}-x^{\frac{1}{2}}+2\right)\,\mathrm{d}x\\ &= \int x^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x-\int x^{\frac{1}{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x+2\int 1\,\mathrm{d}x\\ &= \left(\frac{x^{2+1}}{(2+1)}\right)-\left(\frac{x^{\frac{1}{2}+1}}{(\frac{1}{2}+1)}\right)\\ &\quad +2\left(\frac{x^{0+1}}{(0+1)}\right)+C\\ &= \frac{x^{3}}{3}-\frac{2\sqrt{x^{3}}}{3}+2x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Integrating Sums of Power Functions

question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the sum and constant factor rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}& \int\left(4x^{7}+\sqrt[5]{x}-\frac{1}{\sqrt[7]{x^{13}}}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x\\ &= \int\left(4x^{7}+x^{\frac{1}{5}}-x^{\frac{-13}{7}}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x\\ &= 4\int x^{7}\,\mathrm{d}x+\int x^{\frac{1}{5}}\,\mathrm{d}x-\int x^{\frac{-13}{7}}\,\mathrm{d}x\\ &= 4\left(\frac{x^{7+1}}{(7+1)}\right)+\left(\frac{x^{\frac{1}{5}+1}}{(\frac{1}{5}+1)}\right)\\ &\quad -\left(\frac{x^{\frac{-13}{7}+1}}{(\frac{-13}{7}+1)}\right)+C\\ &= \frac{x^{8}}{2}+\frac{5\sqrt[5]{x^{6}}}{6}+\frac{7}{6\sqrt[7]{x^{6}}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$
